newsitem.title: FRANCE: OECD meets on shipbuilding pact.
newsitem.headline: OECD meets on shipbuilding pact.

text.p: OECD officials began two days of talks on Thursday to try to agree on terms to cut government subsidies to shipbuilders, an OECD spokeswoman said.
The meeting was attended by all members of the shipbuilding committee of the Organisation for Economic Co-Operation and Development, including a delegation from the United States.
Washington is the only capital which has not ratified the Shipbuilding Trade Agreement Act as it stands.
The U.S. House of Representatives on June 13 passed a bill to implement the agreement, but attached an amendment to delay U.S. implementation of the deal by 30 months to January, 1999.
Other signatory nations have said the amendment would violate the pact and said they would not be willing to renegotiate. Those nations have already passed implementing legislation.
The Clinton administration has said it opposes the amendment and the Senate is considering legislation which does not include the delaying amendment.
Washington has been roundly criticised for delaying the pact.

In Brussels, the European Commission said Washington's failure to ratify the agreement created a great deal of uncertainty about its future and urged "common sense to prevail so that tax-payers on both sides of the atlantic are spared needless expense".
A commission spokesman said U.S. ratification was being blocked "by strong vested interests which seek to benefit from large subsidies to re-enter the market for merchant vessels".
"The community remains convinced of the need to establish a level playing field in this sector by eliminating unfair practices such as subsidies or injurious prices," he said
Under the agreement the United States, which does not subsidise shipbuilding, would phase out some of its $50 million a year in federally-backed loan guarantees to the industry.
Virginia Republican Herbert Bateman, author of the amendment, said the delay was needed to equalise clauses that other signatories have negotiated to ease their transition into the agreement.

The amendment also states that the agreement does not affect the Jones Act, which prohibits cargo shipment between U.S. ports in foreign-built ships. The Clinton administration has said the Jones Act exemption was implicit in the agreement.
The amendment also states that private vessels that are used by the U.S. military are exempt from the agreement.
